blocks.text: Jory Ashdown saw it upside down across Foolscap's counter, the way he saw most things that were none of his business: a sunburst stamp with a date ring round it, and on the rim, in letters he knew only from the title pages of Almanacs, the words ZERO POST.
The date in the ring said CS 139. The paper under it was a copy of a charter, granting the site of Octavo to the Folio Assay Company before anybody had built an Octavo to grant.
A small, square, white-haired woman slapped the copy flat with one palm and looked the three of them over like freight.
"Courier," she said to the captain. "You'll do."
Beside Jory, the captain had gone very still. Then he went very polite.
"Madam," he said. "I don't think we've been introduced."
"Don't need to be. Bettina Marr. Dockmaster, Octavo." She said it like an address she still expected letters at. "You're the cutter in from Quarto. You run the far side."
"We've run it," said the captain. "We've nothing booked."
"You have now."

Jory had come up to the counter with the Bishop still in his belt and a cargo docket in his hand, to ask whether Foolscap had anything going inward, and the answer had been no every morning since Lettice walked down their gangway. He put the docket away. It seemed the least he could do.
Soph had already turned the charter copy the right way round. Soph read things the way other people snatched them.
"That's not what you're hiring us for," she said. "That's done."

"That's done," Bettina agreed. "That took the site. The site's not the berth." She laid a second sheet on top, a lease gone soft at the folds. "Ice berth, out on the ring past Octavo. The berth's on the ice, and the ice was never on the site, so the Combine's only ever held it by lease. Lease runs out the first hour of the ninth of Rime. Octavo reckoning, says so in the lease. After that hour it's anybody's."
"Open Post," said Soph. "First valid claim delivered at any office takes it."

"Any office." Bettina showed a good many teeth. "Folio never renews. Folio lets it lapse and claims it fresh, first in the queue, because a claim's cheaper than rent. This time somebody stands in front of them."
"Why us?" said the captain.

"Because water's the last thing on the far side we've still a claim to. Lose the berth and Octavo's a word people say at funerals." She tapped the lease. "And because you've been to Quarto this season, and nobody else in this dock would look at me twice."
"Quarto," said Soph slowly, in the voice of someone hearing a sum begin.

"Water first," said Bettina. "Then the other thing. Our founding declaration gives Octavo's people the right to petition for our standing back, inside twenty years of losing it. Our years, by our calendar. Twenty years from the day Folio's agreement was signed, and there's little more than one of them left. Only Octavo's own may bring it. Not Folio, not the Board, not some kind courier. Us."

Jory heard her say was signed as though the words had corners on them. He didn't ask. At the word Folio he had found something on the Bishop's handle that needed looking at, and he went on looking at it.
"The exiles' purse pays," said Bettina. "It's not much. It's all of it."

The captain signed her hire chit with his initials and his licence number. That was not how he signed things. He signed things with his whole name, large, as if it were a guarantee. Bettina folded the chit into her coat without reading it.
"Courier," she said, which was apparently all the name he was getting.
Jory Ashdown had the Duchess in pieces on the galley table, because a grease gun is a comfort and Soph was about to do sums.
"First hour, ninth of Rime, Octavo," said Soph. "Under sixty-one, converted here, that's twenty days from now."
"Then we've twenty days," said Jory. "She'll do Quarto in ten without breathing hard. Easy, Duchess."
"Technically, no." Soph stopped herself. "Not technically. Actually, no. Sixty-two moved Octavo by eleven days. The correction nobody asked for. Quarto has sixty-two in its drawer."
Jory thought about that for a while. He thought about it the way he'd think about a noise in the drive he had heard once before, a long time ago, and hoped not to hear again.
"Because we put it there," he said.
"Because we put it there. So at Quarto's counter the berth comes free in nine days. Anywhere still on sixty-one, it's twenty, and by then it's gone."
"They know that too, courier," said Bettina to Soph, and laid a flimsy beside the Duchess's barrel.
"Navigator," said Soph.
"Courier. Folio's dock board, by light, this morning. A Combine courier cleared Folio for Quarto eight days back."

"Then Folio's drawer is still on sixty-one," said Soph, "or they'd sit at their own counter for nine days and never send a soul. They've sent a soul." She pulled the flimsy over. "Combine cutters run sixteen to one at best, and nobody runs Folio to Quarto dry, so she'll stop for mass on the way. She docks at Quarto about four hours after the berth comes free. Give or take her fuel call."
"And us?" said Jory.
"Our usual way, with our usual mass stop? Most of a day behind her."
Jory fitted the Duchess's nozzle back on, slowly, and laughed a little before he'd got the joke out. "So that's the trap."
"That's the trap," said Soph. "Sixty-two hands the berth to whoever's standing at Quarto's counter when the hour turns. And it's the opening, because sixty-two doesn't care who's standing there."
She picked up the charter copy again and frowned at the sunburst as if it had cheated at cards.
"And this is wrong," she said. "The Zero Post doesn't take mail. It stamps Almanacs. Every edition, on the title page, so they speak from the Landing. It doesn't stamp charters for mining companies."
"It stamped that one," said Bettina. "In thirty-nine."
"And Octavo was founded in forty-one," said Soph. "So somebody granted your site two years before you were on it."
"Then somebody should have asked why."
"Somebody should," said Bettina, and looked at nobody in particular, which in a galley that size meant everybody.

Behind them the captain had taken a cloth to the manifest board. Jory had watched him clean it an hour ago. It had been clean then. It was very clean now. In the last hour the captain had thanked Soph for her tables, and Bettina for her flimsy, and Waybill for nothing whatsoever, and the politer he got, the more Jory wanted to put the Duchess back together and go and sit in the drive space with the hatch shut.
"Nine days," said the captain, to the board. "We'll be there."
Peregrine Blott bought the spool on Foolscap's low dock, from a chandler who sold rope, mostly, and asked no questions, entirely.
It cost a season of fees. He paid it out of his own account and did not look at what was left.
"Captain," said Jory, at his shoulder, holding the reel as if it might bite. It was black, with no tag, and lighter than a Post spool. "We've two Post spools in the locker."
"The run's spools."
"She's paying."
"For carriage. Not for the Inspector to read 'private hire' on a spool tag at her next audit."
"And if the Inspector reads this?" Jory turned the reel in his hands. "You know what it is if she finds it. A fine and an endorsement."
"I know."

Peregrine had never told Jory about the other one: the opened cask, held on the Inspector's file, unentered, waiting for exactly this. Found together, they would suspend his licence. He did not mention it now.
"Then why—"
"We're running her straight," said Peregrine. "Top of her range, no mass stop. If she coughs out there, I want a line home."
Jory took one of his long pauses. "A cold drive grounds it."
"Then we cask before she's cold."
"One in four's dead," said the chandler, to the rope. "No refunds. Not my thread."

They filed at Foolscap's office before noon. Jory moored the black spool to the Datum Post in the office yard, a squat brass pillar with a fogged clock face, and the thread came off the reel the way good thread did, fine and grey and then not there at all.
Jory put one finger under it, the way he'd test a stay on a rig, and plucked.
It rang flat.
Not the clean note a Post spool gave. A short sour note, like a cracked cup. The thread went slack against the pillar, thin as cobweb, and then it was gone, and Jory was holding an empty reel.
"Dead," said Jory.
Peregrine looked at the reel for exactly as long as it deserved.
"Right," he said. "Back aboard."
Jory said nothing on the walk back. He took his spanner out of his pocket and put it back again, and did not tell it anything.
Waybill spoke as they came through the hatch.
"Mass discrepancy, Captain. Two hundred and twelve grams, arriving with the engineer. No Post tag. No sender. No addressee."
"It's a reel," said Peregrine.
"A reel of what, Captain?"
"Of nothing, now."
"Logged," said Waybill. "One reel, empty, unlicensed. I am obliged to say that possession of an unlicensed spool is a fine and an endorsement."
"Then say it."
"I have said it, Captain. It is in the ship's record, where everything is."
Peregrine left it there. The ship's record was ship's law. An audit could not compel it, only a court on warrant, and no court had a reason to ask.
By the time Foolscap's clamps let go, the reel was parts in Jory's tray, and Waybill had logged each part by mass without comment, which was its comment.
Peregrine Blott let Soph and Jory have the argument, because they were going to have it anyway and it was better had before the drive was hot.
"Twenty all the way," said Soph. "Straight line, no stop. We dock at Quarto three hours before the berth comes free."
"With mass for a sneeze," said Jory.
"A small sneeze."
"She doesn't like the top of her range, Soph. Not for a whole haul. She'll do it. She'll not forgive us."
"She's a ship. She hasn't got feelings."
"She's got a drive, and the drive's got feelings." Jory laughed before he'd finished. "And if she coughs out there, we've no line home now."
That was true, and for a moment everyone looked at the place where the black reel wasn't.
"Take it straight," said Peregrine.
Bettina, wedged at the end of the galley with the claim on her knees, uncapped a pen. "Then I'll sign it now and have done."

"You will not," said Soph. "Anything you seal before we dock is dated before the berth comes free. Here, it's Foolscap's date. Under drive it's ship's reckoning, which is Foolscap's date with a few hours on. Either way it's a claim on a berth that's still under lease, and a claim on a leased berth is a claim on nothing."
"Sealed after docking," said Waybill, "an item takes the dock office's date and hour. At Quarto, that is Quarto's."
"So you sign at Quarto," said Soph. "After the hour. Not on it, after it. Then you hand it in the hour after that, because a delivery in the same hour as its postmark is void."
"Two hours of standing about," said Bettina.
"Their agent stands about the same two, or theirs is nothing too. And they're four hours behind us. If she holds."
Bettina looked at each of them in turn, and at the speaker over the hatch.
"Hollow it," she said, "the lot of you," and capped the pen. Somewhere around the words ship's reckoning, Peregrine noticed, she had stopped calling Soph courier.
They ran her straight.

Postscript went to the top of her range with a hum in the hull that Peregrine had never liked, and Jory sat in the drive space with the hatch open, talking to the drive under his breath as if it were a horse. Nobody in the Drift could hear them, and they could hear nobody. Peregrine kept the manifest board on the mass gauge and did not wipe it once.
They came off drive at Quarto with the gauge in the red and docked in grace, early, exactly where Soph had said they would.

Quarto's office smelled of soil. Ko's beans were on the sill, but Ko was not behind the counter; the clerk said he was up-ring and would be some days. Peregrine left him a note and did not write what it was about.
They waited aboard for the hour. Bettina sat at the galley table with the claim in front of her and the pen in her fist, and watched the clock as if it owed her money.
"The lease has lapsed, by Quarto's drawer," said Waybill. Then, after a long hour, "It is now the following hour, Quarto reckoning."
Bettina signed. She sealed it herself, pressing hard.
"Sealed after docking," said Waybill. "Postmark: Quarto dock office. Logged."

She carried it to the counter on her own, with Peregrine a pace behind, and stood there with it held against her coat until the next hour came up on the counter clock. Then she handed it across. The clerk checked the dock office's mark against the counter clock, punched the claim, entered it, and gave the punched original back to her. First on the berth.
Soph put her head in at the door. "Combine courier's just got her clamps. Four hours behind, near enough. My table was right."
"Still on time," said Peregrine.
Bettina held the punched claim flat against her coat with both hands. For a moment she looked every one of her years, and then she didn't.
"Water," she said. "Octavo's got its water."
Jory Ashdown came up to Quarto's counter with Margaret in his pocket, because he'd run the drive into the red for that punch and wanted to look at what he'd bought.
Bettina had not left the counter. She had the claim in one hand and was asking the clerk for something else.
"The charter," she said. "Octavo's site, to the Folio Assay Company. I want its Register entry. All of it. For the other thing."
The clerk brought the entry up from the shared register and turned the screen to face her. Bettina read it aloud, slowly, the way you'd read a list of who hadn't come home.
"Postmark, Zero Post, CS 139. Delivered at the Concordat Register, Gnomon, CS 153. Valid. Punched. Entered. Delivering courier, Second Class." She read out a licence number.
Jory knew that number. He had copied it onto every docket he had ever filed.
"Name of Blott," read Bettina.
She took the hire chit out of her coat and unfolded it beside the screen: two initials, and the same number.
The captain stood very straight at Jory's side. His hand had found the little chain that held the counter's pen, and it was straightening the chain, though the chain had been straight.
Bettina did not look at the chit again. She looked at him.
"Blott," she said. "You're the Blott who carried our charter."
